data.name: Latvia
data.summary: Capital gains taxed at 25.5% (from 2025) plus a 3% surtax on income above EUR 200k; foreign and domestic dividends that were taxed at source are PIT-exempt (but count for the 3% surtax); no inheritance, gift-to-children or wealth tax. Companies pay 20/80 CIT only on distribution.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence
regimes.description: Ordinary Latvian tax residence; no special regime for new wealthy arrivals.
regimes.eligibility: Declared place of residence in Latvia, or 183 days in any 12-month period.

capital_gains.summary: Capital gains on shares, funds, bonds, real estate and crypto are taxed at 25.5% (since 1 Jan 2025, up from 20%), plus the 3% additional rate on total annual income above EUR 200,000, so 28.5% at the margin for a large gain.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Latvian real estate: exempt if held 60 months and declared primary residence for 12 months, or held 60 months as the only property, or proceeds reinvested in a like property within 12 months. Capital losses offset capital gains (crypto separately).
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Investment account (ieguldījumu konts): income is taxed only when withdrawals exceed deposits (PIT Law Section 11.9(11)(6) and the rule that follows it), so a listed portfolio can be rolled over without tax until money is taken out.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Transactions begun but not completed by 31 Dec 2024 and notified to the SRS remain at 20% in 2025-2027. Section 15(5) of the PIT Law: 25.5% on income from capital, including capital gains. Section 15.1 (in force 1 Jan 2026 wording): an additional 3% on the excess of total annual income over EUR 200,000, payable through the annual return; the base expressly includes taxable income 'including capital gains and income from capital' and the dividends and liquidation quotas exempted by Section 9(1)(2.1)-(2.2).

income_surtax.notes: Additional rate (PIT Law §15.1, from 1 January 2026): 3% on the excess of a person's total income over EUR 200,000 a year, where total income includes capital gains and the dividends exempt under §9(1)(2.1); per taxpayer (no joint filing). Not indexed.

capital_gains.rate_basis: 25.5% capital income rate + 3% additional rate on income above EUR 200k = 28.5% for a large gain; no holding-period relief except the main-home/sole-property exemption. Investment account can defer tax on listed portfolios. 25.5% on capital income (§15(5)); the 3% additional rate above EUR 200,000 per person is in income_surtax.
capital_gains.professional_trader: No specific recharacterisation regime found; business income of a self-employed person is taxed at progressive rates (25.5%/33%) plus social contributions.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: Securities: none. Latvian real estate: 60 months for the residence/sole-property exemption.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed; foreign tax credited up to Latvian tax on that income.

dividends.summary: Dividends are exempt from PIT when CIT was paid on the distributed profit in Latvia, or when CIT (or an equivalent tax) was paid abroad or PIT/WHT was withheld abroad on the dividend (PIT Law Section 9(1)(2.1)); otherwise taxed at 25.5%. Tax-haven dividends are always taxed. Even exempt dividends count toward the 3% additional rate on income above EUR 200,000 (Section 15.1(2)).
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: Exemption needs evidence of foreign CIT or WHT (EU/EEA companies generally excepted from proof, but SRS may ask).
dividends.important_exceptions: Ordinary foreign portfolio dividends that suffered source WHT (e.g. 15% US treaty WHT) or come from a company that paid CIT abroad are exempt, not taxed at 25.5% with a credit: the statute settles the conflict with a broker article (TWINO) that described a credit method. An additional 3% PIT applies to the part of total annual income above EUR 200,000, and the base includes exempt dividends. From 2026 Latvian companies wholly owned by individuals may opt into a 15% CIT + 6% PIT dividend regime.

regimes.name: Latvian holding company (SIA)
regimes.description: The family holds the portfolio through a Latvian private limited company (SIA) owned by the parents. Latvia taxes a company's profit only when it is distributed or deemed distributed: 20% of the gross-up (net distribution divided by 0.8), i.e. 25% of the net amount. Dividends and gains the SIA earns and keeps are untaxed. A resident individual shareholder pays no personal income tax on a dividend from profit on which Latvian company income tax was paid (PIT Law Section 9(1)(2.1)(a)), but the exempt dividend still counts toward the 3% additional rate on a person's total annual income above EUR 200,000 (Section 15.1). Wealth tax (none) and inheritance tax (none) are the same as for direct holding, so they inherit from the standard regime.
regimes.eligibility: Any person can found an SIA (articles, Commercial Register entry). The shareholders must be Latvian tax residents for the personal-side treatment modelled here. Contributing an existing portfolio in kind is a disposal for the individual (tax at 25.5% on the gain under PIT Law Section 15(5), not verified for contributions to capital); the structure is cheapest funded with cash or newly bought positions.
regimes.duration_note: A company under ordinary law with no time limit; the distribution-based system has no sunset in the sources read.

structure.entity: sabiedrība ar ierobežotu atbildību (SIA, private limited company)
structure.payout_notes: Company income tax of 20% on the grossed-up distribution (net / 0.8), so 20% of the cash the company uses (EUR 80 paid out costs EUR 20 of tax on a EUR 100 outlay; PwC). The shareholder's dividend is exempt from personal income tax (PIT Law Section 9(1)(2.1)(a)), but counts toward the additional 3% rate on a taxpayer's total annual income above EUR 200,000 (Section 15.1(1),(2)): 3% x 80 = 2.4 per 100 of outlay at the top marginal rate, so payout_tax_rate = 0.20 + 0.024 = 0.224. A couple sharing a EUR 400,000 net payout equally sits at the EUR 200,000 threshold per person; the threshold is not indexed, and the top marginal case is assumed. Liquidation quota is exempt from PIT where Latvian company tax was paid (Section 9(1)(2.2)). Since 1 January 2026 an SIA owned only by individuals may opt for an alternative: 15% company tax on net/0.85 plus 6% PIT withheld on the dividend (PIT Law Section 15(5.1); Corporate Income Tax Law Article 4.2). Not modelled: per EUR 100 received it costs about 28.3 against 28.0 for the standard route if the 3% rate also applies, so it is not better.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Deemed distributions are taxed at the 20/80 rate when they arise: non-business expenses, loans to related parties (with exclusions), excess interest, transfer-pricing adjustments, hybrid mismatches, assets transferred abroad (PwC). Private use of company assets or loans to the shareholders therefore costs 25% of the net amount. Dividends to tax-haven recipients are always taxed. No substance test is needed for a resident SIA holding a portfolio.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: On liquidation, surplus assets are a deemed distribution taxed at 20/80 (PwC); the liquidation quota is then PIT-exempt for the shareholder (Section 9(1)(2.2)). Exit tax on an individual who emigrates with SIA shares was not researched.

income.name: Latvia

income_tax.summary: Progressive resident income tax: 25.5% up to EUR 105,300 of annual income, 33% above, and an additional 3% on the part above EUR 200,000 (first applied in 2026 for 2025 income), recorded as 36%. Fixed personal allowance EUR 550 a month (EUR 6,600 a year, PwC deductions page), applied regardless of income; dependant allowance EUR 250 a month not modelled. Employee state social insurance contributions (NSIC) 10.50% (9.25% for those eligible for retirement), income capped at EUR 105,300; minimum wage EUR 780 a month in 2026.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed NSIC 31.07% (29.36% if eligible for retirement) on income up to EUR 105,300, with minimum contributions based on the EUR 780 monthly minimum wage. Sole traders may apply for micro-enterprise tax status (details in the PwC corporate summary, not opened) and apply the fixed personal allowance to PIT-subject income. Self-employed persons with income below three minimum monthly wages a quarter can opt to pay 10% NSIC on actual income (PwC). Employee social_security_deductible: Rests on a secondary guide (no VID or statute page opened); medium confidence.

succession.name: Latvia
succession.summary: Latvian law guarantees close relatives a reserved share, paid in money. A foreign resident can choose the law of their nationality (EU Succession Regulation art. 22). Latvia has no trusts, and foundations exist, but private-benefit use is not confirmed.
succession.reserved_share: Persons entitled to a reserved share (Civil Law, Art. 423 as amended 2014) can claim its value in money. The page does not give who or what fraction, and it was not found elsewhere.

succession.trust_note: Latvia is not in the HCCH table for the 1985 Trusts Convention. Trusts have not been introduced in Latvian law. Foundations are governed by the Law on Associations and Foundations; no profit may be distributed, and private-benefit use was not confirmed.

assumptions: The family are Latvian tax residents from arrival (declared residence or 183 days) and EU citizens needing no permit.

Top marginal case for the personal and payout figures: every euro of income is above the EUR 200,000 threshold of the 3% additional rate, which applies per taxpayer. With a EUR 400,000 net payout shared by two spouses the SIA payout is at the threshold; the threshold is not indexed, so over 60 years it is crossed in nominal terms.
Personal path: gains taxed when realised at 25.5%. The investment account is not modelled (see open questions).
SIA path: funded with cash or newly bought positions; the SIA distributes only what the family spends and keeps and compounds the rest untaxed.
Foreign dividends carry 15% withholding in the checks; they are PIT-exempt for the individual and the withholding is lost inside the SIA.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: the investment account (PIT Law Sections 11.9(11)(6), 11.9(12.2), 11.13): income from the account arises only when money paid out exceeds the money paid in, less taxed or exempt dividends and interest earned in it; purchases and sales inside it are not taxable events. Only cash (or securities moved from another investment account, or acquired inside the account) may be paid in (Section 11.13(4)), through a provider in Latvia, the EU, EEA, OECD or a treaty state (Section 11.13(3)). With a EUR 30m cash contribution and EUR 400,000 withdrawn a year, withdrawals would not pass contributions for decades, so the 25.5% (28.5%) gains tax could be deferred for the whole projection; the engine taxes realised gains each year and has no contribution ledger.

Dividends of the SIA paid to a resident individual: whether the 3% additional rate really applies to a dividend exempt under Section 9(1)(2.1) is as read in Section 15.1(2)(2); the SRS explanation was not opened.

Optional regime for individually owned companies (PIT Law Section 15(5.1), Corporate Income Tax Law Article 4.2): 15% company tax on net/0.85 plus 6% PIT withheld. Worked from PwC's description, per EUR 100 received it costs about 28.3 against 28.0 for the standard route, if the 3% rate also applies to such dividends (taxable income counts under Section 15.1(2)(1)); if it did not, the option would be cheaper by about 2.8. The Corporate Income Tax Law text and the SRS explanation of 27 July 2026 were not opened, and a Finance Ministry note seen in a search result gave 2028 as the start; not modelled.
The SIA's running costs are not in the tax file, so the SIA check carries none. The Corporate Income Tax Law text (rate, deemed distributions) was not opened; PwC (reviewed 30 June 2026) was used.

Structures considered and not modelled: a private family foundation or trust (not researched). Funding the SIA with an existing portfolio in kind is a disposal for the individual (not verified for contributions to capital).

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally (ordinary residence)
paths.note: 25.5% on capital gains and a 3% additional rate on total income above EUR 200,000 a year (PIT Law Sections 15(5), 15.1). Dividends from foreign companies are PIT-exempt where tax was withheld abroad (Section 9(1)(2.1)(b)) but still count toward the 3% rate. No wealth, inheritance or gift tax. The investment account (ieguldījumu konts) would defer the gains tax, but the engine cannot express it, so it is not a path.

paths.name: Latvian holding company (SIA)
paths.note: The SIA pays no tax on dividends and gains it retains; company income tax of 20% on the grossed-up amount (25% of the net) is due only when it distributes. The shareholder's dividend is PIT-exempt (Section 9(1)(2.1)(a)) but counts toward the 3% additional rate above EUR 200,000. The parents' estate holds the SIA shares at about the portfolio's value; Latvia has no inheritance tax, so there is no business-relief question. The optional 15%/6% regime for individually owned companies is not modelled (about the same cost, see the tax file).

immigration.name: Latvia
immigration.summary: EU citizens register their residence. Non-EU nationals lost the property and bank-deposit residence routes when the new Immigration Law took effect on 15 September 2026; the remaining investor route is EUR 50,000 (EUR 100,000 for larger firms) in a Latvian company's share capital plus a EUR 10,000 state payment, and a EUR 150,000 fund route that is not operational yet. Russian and Belarusian citizens are barred from investor permits. A remote-work visa exists but its income threshold is unverified.
immigration.naturalisation: Reported as 10 years of legal residence, the last 5 on a permanent residence permit, with Latvian language (A2) and history/constitution tests and legal income. The 10-year figure comes from secondary guides; an official PMLP brochure speaks only of 5 years of permanent residence. Not verified against the Citizenship Law.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: Dual citizenship is allowed on naturalisation for citizens of EU, EFTA and NATO states and some others; other nationalities may be asked to renounce (secondary sources, not verified against the law).
